Pregnancy

Your waters have broken, but contractions have not started

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

If your waters may have broken, contact your maternity team now, even if you feel well and have no contractions. A gap before labour can happen, but the next step depends on your pregnancy stage and an assessment. Do not wait a day before making the first call.

Make the first call when you suspect a leak

Contact your midwife, obstetric team or maternity triage service as soon as you think your waters have broken, even if the fluid is clear and there are no contractions. Do not wait 24 hours before calling. If you are less than 37 weeks pregnant, prompt hospital assessment is needed whether or not you have pain.

Use a clean sanitary or maternity pad, not a tampon. Note when the leaking began, how much there is and its colour and smell. Tell the team about your baby’s movements and any bleeding, fever or pain. If you are unsure whether the fluid is urine, ordinary discharge or waters, that uncertainty is a reason to ask for assessment rather than delay.

If you have no regular pregnancy clinician, contact the nearest maternity unit or hospital. Use emergency services for severe symptoms or when you need emergency help reaching care. Not having received antenatal care should never keep you from seeking help now.

What it means when the membranes rupture

Your baby develops within a sac of membranes containing amniotic fluid. When an opening forms in those membranes, fluid can pass through the cervix and out of the vagina. This is called rupture of membranes. An obvious gush and a small ongoing trickle can both represent a leak; a small amount is not automatically a minor problem.

Waters often break during labour, but they can break before labour begins. Prelabour rupture of membranes, or PROM, describes that timing. If it happens before 37 completed weeks, it is called preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, or PPROM. At 37 weeks or later, it is term PROM.

Sometimes membranes are deliberately opened by a clinician as part of a planned induction or labour care. That procedure is different from an unexpected leak at home. Do not try to open the membranes yourself or check inside your vagina to find out what is happening.

Why contractions may not begin straight away

Contractions and rupture of membranes do not always happen in the same order. There may be a period between the first leak and established labour, or early tightenings may be mild enough that you barely notice them. No pain does not prove that the membranes are intact.

Many people begin labour naturally after their waters break, but the timing varies. An average duration quoted for a first labour is not a prediction of how long you can safely wait after a leak. The important questions are how far along you are, how long the membranes have been ruptured and whether you or the baby have any concerns.

Membranes are part of the barrier against infection. Once they have ruptured, the time to birth becomes relevant to infection risk. This is why the team may recommend induction or closer observation even while you feel well. A lack of contractions alone does not establish that waiting is safe.

Assessment can clarify the leak and the next step

The team asks about the fluid loss, pregnancy history, symptoms and fetal movements, and checks your observations and your baby’s wellbeing. Depending on the circumstances, they may use a sterile speculum to look for fluid and a fluid test if the diagnosis is uncertain. An ultrasound can add information but does not always settle the diagnosis by itself.

Tell them about a previous preterm birth or PPROM, a known short cervix, bleeding in this pregnancy, multiple pregnancy or a baby known to be breech or sideways. Bring any group B streptococcus result and mention if a previous baby had GBS infection. These details can change the plan.

If the first assessment does not confirm rupture but leaking continues, contact the team again. Before leaving, get clear instructions about whom to call overnight, when to return and what would require an earlier review. Being sent home after assessment should include a plan, not simply waiting indefinitely for pain.

Options when you are at least 37 weeks pregnant

When assessment finds no other concern at term, the team discusses beginning labour medically or allowing a short period for it to start on its own. Your preferences matter alongside the findings. For example, NICE guidance offers induction as soon as possible or expectant management for up to approximately 24 hours, then offers induction if labour has not started.

That 24-hour interval is a treatment discussion after contact and assessment, not a deadline for making your first call. If you decide to wait longer, discuss the changing risks and agree an ongoing monitoring and birth plan with the team. Contractions, fever, bleeding or altered fetal movements can change the recommendation before the planned review time.

GBS can also change the timing. NICE recommends immediate induction at term after a positive GBS result in the current pregnancy or a previous baby affected by GBS, with caesarean birth if it was already planned. The team also considers antibiotics during labour. A GBS result does not automatically mean every person needs a caesarean.

Ask what induction would involve for you, where you should give birth and whether your baby may need extra observation afterward. A previous caesarean, another pregnancy complication or local maternity policy can affect the details.

Before 37 weeks, care balances infection and prematurity

PPROM requires assessment without waiting for contractions. It is less common than term rupture; RCOG patient information describes it in up to about 3% of pregnancies. The very broad figures sometimes quoted online should not be used to estimate your personal risk.

The team weighs the risks of infection and other complications against the risks of being born early. If you and the baby are well, pregnancy may sometimes continue with close supervision. If infection, a problem with the baby or another serious concern develops, earlier birth may be the safer option. There is no single waiting interval that applies at every gestation.

You may initially need hospital observation. Depending on gestation and the likelihood of early birth, care can include antibiotics, corticosteroid injections to reduce complications of prematurity, or magnesium sulfate to protect a very preterm baby’s brain. These treatments have different purposes; not everyone needs every medicine.

Rupture very early in pregnancy needs an individual specialist discussion about possible outcomes and available care. Ask to speak with the neonatal team when appropriate. If a home-care plan is offered after assessment, make sure you understand its follow-up schedule and when to return immediately.

Possible contributors are not a reason to blame yourself

Often there is no single identifiable reason why waters break early. Infection, placental problems or other pregnancy complications may contribute. Tell the team about an injury, a procedure or any known concern about excess amniotic fluid, rather than deciding that one of these must explain the leak.

Factors associated with preterm birth include previous preterm birth, a short cervix, pregnancy bleeding, smoking, low weight before pregnancy and dietary deficiencies. These factors do not diagnose PPROM, predict exactly when a baby will arrive or prove that something you did caused it. Many people who give birth early have no recognized risk factor.

Support for nutrition and stopping smoking can be useful parts of pregnancy care, but they cannot repair an already ruptured membrane or replace assessment. After a previous PPROM or preterm birth, ask about a tailored plan in a future pregnancy. The focus should be useful care and support, not blame.

Rest, food and bathing while following the plan

If the team advises waiting at home, rest and use the gentle activity plan they recommend. A short comfortable walk may be appropriate for some people, but walking is not a requirement to make labour start, and advice after PPROM may differ. Keep your phone, contact number and transport arrangements ready.

Drink and eat according to the instructions you are given. There is no universal rule that everyone must stop eating the moment waters break or that every hospital admission means fasting. Procedures, medicines and the possibility of surgery can change that advice.

At term, NICE advises that ordinary bathing or showering is not associated with increased infection, whereas vaginal intercourse may increase it. Follow individualized advice, especially if the waters broke preterm, and never delay assessment to take a bath. Avoid vaginal sex, tampons and inserting products while awaiting the agreed care.

Use pads to observe the loss, follow instructions for checking your temperature and keep track of your baby’s usual movements. Do not try home induction methods or take leftover antibiotics. Monitoring is useful only when you also know what changes to report and can reach the team.

Changes that override the waiting plan

Contact maternity care urgently for green or brown fluid, an unpleasant smell, fresh bleeding, fever or chills, persistent abdominal pain, reduced baby movements or feeling increasingly unwell. Do not wait for contractions to reach a certain interval if any of these occur.

Call emergency services for heavy bleeding, collapse or a possible umbilical cord in the vagina. If you can see or feel something that may be the cord, do not touch it or try to push it back. Tell the dispatcher you are pregnant and suspect cord prolapse.

While waiting for emergency help for suspected cord prolapse, get onto your knees with your chest lowered toward the floor and your hips raised, if you can, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. This is an uncommon emergency but needs rapid care.

If contractions start without warning signs, follow the arrival instructions already agreed with your team. If they do not start by the planned review time, make contact as arranged. It is understandable to feel excited, anxious or both; asking for a clear plan and support is part of getting ready safely.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Term PROM and preterm PROM require different decisions. Immediate contact is separate from an agreed period of waiting after assessment.

Guidance considers gestation, infection, GBS, fetal wellbeing and the person’s preferences. Local policies may differ.

Preterm-birth risk factors do not establish the cause of an individual membrane rupture.

How BeMama can help

Keep the time of the first leak, symptoms, contact number and agreed return time together. BeMama tracking must not delay maternity assessment or emergency care.

When to seek help

Call maternity care promptly for suspected waters breaking. Before 37 weeks, seek prompt hospital assessment. Reduced movements, fever, abnormal-smelling or green/brown fluid, bleeding or persistent pain need urgent contact; heavy bleeding, collapse or suspected cord prolapse requires emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Call when leaking waters are suspected; contractions are not required.
  • Before 37 weeks, prompt hospital assessment is needed.
  • A term waiting period must be an agreed plan with monitoring and a return time.
  • New warning signs take priority over a planned appointment or contraction interval.

Frequently asked questions

Can my waters break without pain?

Yes. Membranes can rupture before contractions begin. A painless trickle still needs maternity advice.

What if I think it might just be urine?

Use a pad, note the loss and call your maternity team. Appearance or smell at home cannot reliably settle the diagnosis.

Should I wait 24 hours before calling?

No. Call when you first suspect rupture. A roughly 24-hour waiting option at term is discussed after assessment, when appropriate.

Does rupture mean I will definitely need induction?

Not always. Labour may start spontaneously. Gestation, time since rupture, infection risk and your baby’s wellbeing guide the recommendation.

What changes if I am 36 weeks pregnant?

That is before 37 completed weeks, so it is preterm. Seek prompt hospital assessment even without contractions; term waiting advice should not be applied to yourself.

Does a positive GBS result mean a caesarean?

Not automatically. It can change the timing of birth and antibiotic advice. The method of birth depends on your obstetric circumstances and any existing plan.

Can I have a bath or shower?

At term, NICE does not associate ordinary bathing or showering with increased infection. Follow your team’s individual advice, especially after preterm rupture, and do not postpone assessment to bathe.

Did poor nutrition or something I did cause this?

You cannot determine that from a risk-factor list. Many cases have no clear cause, and associations do not establish blame. Discuss any support you need with the team.

When should I return before the agreed time?

Seek urgent advice for reduced movements, fever or chills, changed or foul-smelling fluid, bleeding, persistent pain or feeling unwell. Heavy bleeding, collapse or a possible cord in the vagina requires emergency services.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
